comments.author: dmiladinov
comments.why: Linus on natural hierarchy in kernel development.
comments.text: I'd like to piggy-back on your mention of Linus. It reminds me of a recent video I saw wherein he talked about how the work on the kernel works within a natural hierarchy. The whole video, IMHO is worth a watch, but the relevant snippet is here, you can watch from about 15:57 to about 18:20 to get the idea: [VIDEO] I especially liked his comment at the end of this section: "The way people work ... is inherent in our brains ... the whole development process ... works really well ... we used the hierarchy that just worked on its own, and that turns out to be the right hierarchy."

comments.author: throwaway1194
comments.why: Linus on benefits of a shared kernel.
comments.text: > I think that makes some sense for performance, too: people run databases where IO efficiency eventually translates to money saved every month, and then we desktop users benefit from many of those as well. Indeed, that's a huge advantage of Linux, the fact that we all run the same Linux kernel and benefit from improvements coming from all directions. Linus himself mentions this advantage here: [VIDEO] There's a nice recent benchmark here (Bcachefs vs. Btrfs vs. EXT4 vs. F2FS vs. XFS): [LINK] Bcachefs is starting to look really good against Btrfs, no APFS or ZFS though, but still interesting nonetheless.

comments.author: dijit
comments.story: Next steps for Rust in the kernel
comments.why: Linus on C mapping closely to assembly.
comments.text: Steve Klabnik has done a lot for systems programming and that post is a lot more even-handed than you're suggesting. If, however, we're talking about the kernel then perhaps we should listen to what Torvalds says about this topic. "People who designed C, designed it at a time where the language had to be geared towards the output, so when I read C I can think about the Assembly that it will create": [VIDEO] Consider that he said this in a time with C++, even if Rust was in its infancy: it is not as tied to the assembly it produces. Not by a long shot.

comments.text: Linus seems to disagree with you. Albeit old [VIDEO] It remains true. If you can reason with -O0 you can take it that your code will remain correct in later levels.

comments.author: pmilot
comments.why: Linus as experienced C programmer on C's merits.
comments.text: That's an unfair judgement toward the C development community as a whole. There are legitimate use cases for C. If you're writing low-level, bare-metal programs then there is no other portable programming language that offers better semantics. C programmers often laud that language because they can easily reason what the output of the compiler will be. That is an extremely important and rare property for a portable programming language. But hey, don't listen to me, listen to an actual experienced C programmer: [VIDEO]
